issues.legal_issue: A person claiming under an unprobated will cannot be substituted as executor, but may be transposed as appellant in the capacity of a legal representative already before the court.
material_facts: After the original appellant died, one respondent sought substitution as the will’s sole executor and as the deceased’s legal representative.
The will had not been probated.
The deceased’s legal representatives were already on the record, and the respondent seeking substitution was one of them.
issues.conclusion: The respondent could not be impleaded as executor under the unprobated will, but could be transposed as appellant as a legal representative.
issues.legal_principle: Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act prevents the respondent from being impleaded in the capacity of executor under an unprobated will. Under Order 22 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the relevant rules of the Court, the respondent could be transposed as appellant because the legal representatives were already on the record. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: special_leave_proceeding and deceased_party and unprobated_will_claimed and claimant_is_legal_representative and legal_representatives_already_on_record

predicates.special_leave_proceeding: The matter is a special leave proceeding in which substitution of a deceased party is sought.
predicates.deceased_party: A party to the proceeding has died.
predicates.unprobated_will_claimed: A person claims to act as executor under a will that has not been probated.
predicates.claimant_is_legal_representative: The person seeking substitution is also a legal representative of the deceased party.
predicates.legal_representatives_already_on_record: The deceased party’s legal representatives are already parties to the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a party dies in a special leave proceeding and an unprobated will is invoked by a claimant who is a legal representative already before the court, that claimant may be transposed as appellant as a legal representative, but not impleaded as executor under the will.

issues.legal_issue: A court may correct an arbitral award to grant consequential possession where the award has conclusively determined ownership, omitted that relief because of an apparent legal mistake, and correction would not alter the arbitrator’s decision.
material_facts: The arbitrator determined that the disputed property was the appellant’s exclusive personal property and rejected the respondents’ claim to an interest in it as partners.

The respondents’ possession was not claimed to arise from a tenancy or protected licence, and no rent or compensation was said to be paid; their claim rested on the rejected partnership-property contention.

The arbitrator omitted consequential possession because he mistakenly considered possession to be governed by rent-control legislation, and directed that possession not be disturbed except by due process of law.
The appellant filed possession suits during the appeal, but did so without prejudice to his appellate rights and out of caution.
The award had determined the parties’ rights, and the arbitrator had died.
issues.conclusion: The Court corrected the award to require the respondents in possession to hand over possession to the appellant’s legal representative. Remitting the award was unnecessary because no matter remained undetermined.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 15(b) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, a court may modify or correct an award that is imperfect in form or contains an obvious error that can be amended without affecting the arbitrator’s decision; it may not substitute its own decision for the award. The award should be made effective and final rather than leave the parties to further litigation. Section 16 remittal was unnecessary because the award had determined the relevant rights and no matter remained undetermined. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: arbitral_award_appeal and ownership_conclusively_determined and occupants_claim_only_rejected_interest and no_protected_occupancy_basis and consequential_relief_omitted_due_to_apparent_error and correction_preserves_award_decision

predicates.arbitral_award_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an arbitral award.
predicates.ownership_conclusively_determined: The award conclusively determines that a property belongs exclusively to one party.
predicates.occupants_claim_only_rejected_interest: The people in possession claim an interest in the property only on a ground that the award rejects.
predicates.no_protected_occupancy_basis: The occupants have no established tenancy, protected licence, or comparable right to remain in possession.
predicates.consequential_relief_omitted_due_to_appa: The award omits relief that follows from its determination because of an apparent mistake about the occupants’ rights.
predicates.correction_preserves_award_decision: The omitted relief can be added without changing the decision made in the award.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an award that conclusively establishes exclusive ownership, rejects the occupants’ only claimed interest, and omits consequential relief because of an apparent error, the award may be corrected to grant that relief if the correction preserves the award’s decision.

issues.legal_issue: A court may resolve a dispute over shared property by directing the parties to follow a fair valuation and buyout arrangement proposed in the proceeding.
material_facts: The arbitrator had determined that the parties held different shares in the disputed tenanted property, and one respondent was in possession.

The respondents proposed that the appellant value the property and that they could either take it on that valuation and pay the appellant’s share, or receive the monetary value of their respective shares.
The Court considered the proposal fair and directed the parties to follow it, including the resulting arrangement for retaining or handing over possession.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the parties to implement the valuation and buyout arrangement, including payment and the resulting transfer or retention of possession.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted the respondents’ proposal as a fair means of resolving the property dispute and issued directions to implement it. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this direction.

predicates.appeal_concerning_shared_property: The appeal concerns property in which the parties have determined shared interests.
predicates.parties_propose_valuation_and_buyout: The parties propose valuing the property and resolving their interests through payment or a buyout.
predicates.court_finds_proposal_fair: The court considers the proposed arrangement fair.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns shared property and the parties propose a valuation and buyout arrangement that the court finds fair, the court orders that arrangement to be implemented.

issues.legal_issue: A party who does not object to transferring possession of property to other co-owners may be directed to hand over the portion in that party’s occupation.
material_facts: The arbitrator had determined that the appellant and two respondents owned the property in equal shares.
The appellant did not object to handing over to the respondents the portion of the property that had been in the appellant’s occupation.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the appellant to hand over possession of the occupied portion to the respondents.
issues.legal_principle: The Court gave effect to the appellant’s stated lack of objection and directed the transfer of possession. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this direction.

predicates.appeal_concerning_co_owned_property: The appeal concerns property determined to be co-owned by the parties.
predicates.party_in_occupation_does_not_object_to_h: A party occupying part of the property does not object to handing that part over to the other co-owners.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns co-owned property and the occupying party does not object to handing over the occupied portion, the court orders possession transferred to the other co-owners.
